name: Velocity based training (VBT)

lead: Velocity-based training (VBT) uses how fast the barbell moves to guide a workout. Instead of fixed percentages of a one-rep max, lifters read bar speed in metres per second and adjust weight or stop a set when speed drops by a set amount.

The appearance link runs through training quality: more consistent loading and managed fatigue can support steady strength and muscle gain, which shape the physique. Meta-analyses have compared VBT with percentage-based programmes mainly on strength, jump and sprint results.

paras: Lifters attach a sensor or use a camera-based app that reports mean or peak bar speed each rep. Some use speed to pick the day's load from a warm-up, others end the set once speed falls by a chosen percentage. It is used on lifts such as squat, bench press and deadlift.
Injury risk is that of resistance training in general. Devices can vary in accuracy, particularly wearables at slow speeds, and large velocity-loss thresholds bring more fatigue.

angle.text: VBT gives lifters objective feedback on each set, which they use to tune training load and fatigue. Over months this supports the progressive training that builds a stronger, more muscular physique.

lead: Velocity-based training (VBT) is a resistance-training method that tracks barbell speed to give feedback and adjust loads in real time. It is mostly applied to compound lifts such as squats, deadlifts, bench press and Olympic lift variations.[1]

Load and bar speed are related in a roughly linear, predictable way, so speed can indicate strength, fatigue and readiness on a given day. Lifters can end sets when speed falls by a set percentage; a 20 percent loss is a common example.[1]

For physique goals, lifters use VBT to keep training intensity matched to daily condition and limit unnecessary fatigue so they can train hard repeatedly, which is the route to added muscle and strength. Research has examined strength, power and in some cases hypertrophy outcomes.[2][3][4]
infobox: Linear position transducers, cameras, apps, wearables

paras: VBT rests on the principle of intent to move: trying to move a load quickly is linked to recruiting high-threshold motor units and building rate of force development.[1] Common measures are mean velocity, mean propulsive velocity and peak velocity.[1]
The minimum velocity threshold, the slowest speed at which a rep can still be completed, is closely tied to a lifter's one-rep max. Lifters can estimate one-rep max from routine training data.[1]

Options include lab motion capture, multi-camera rack systems, linear position transducers (cord-and-spool devices considered valid and reliable), smartphone apps and accelerometer-based wearables. Wearables are portable and inexpensive but can be inconsistent at slow speeds.[1]

Uses include motivation through immediate feedback, fatigue monitoring, autoregulation (comparing warm-up speeds with baselines) and testing.[1] Velocity-loss stops are a common way to end sets; reviews of elite athletes describe 10–20 percent losses being used to induce adaptations while reducing neuromuscular fatigue.[5]

A 2021 systematic review of seven studies in elite athletes found velocity losses of 10–20 percent associated with neuromuscular adaptations and reduced fatigue.[5] A 2021 meta-analysis compared VBT with percentage-based training for strength, jump, sprint and change-of-direction performance.[6] A 2022 meta-analysis of nine controlled trials in 253 trained men reported that VBT may improve lower-limb maximum strength, strength endurance and countermovement jump.[3]

A randomised trial in 16 trained men compared velocity-based and percentage-based loading on strength and jump height.[7] A randomised trial of bench press velocity loss examined strength, neuromuscular adaptation and muscle hypertrophy.[4] Reviews also describe VBT in rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.[8]
Wikipedia's summary notes that velocity losses of 30 percent or more may increase hypertrophy but bring greater fatigue.[1]

VBT appears in training logs on strength forums such as T Nation, where lifters discuss programming around bar speed and fatigue.[9] It is a lifestyle and training topic for physique-focused lifters rather than an appearance product.

timeline.event: Improving bar-speed monitoring begins making VBT easier and cheaper to use.[1]
